justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, starting near 91.5 for the one-day forecast and rising gradually to 93.5 at one month. This gentle appreciation likely reflects a baseline assumption of continued momentum or mean-reversion toward a perceived fair value, combined with whatever macroeconomic backdrop was prevailing at the time of the forecast — likely expectations around interest rate differentials, stable risk appetite, or commodity-linked flows depending on the asset in question. The short-term estimate is anchored heavily by recent price action and inertia, while the longer-term estimates incorporate a slightly more optimistic drift, though not dramatically so, suggesting no major structural break was anticipated.

The confidence interval widths widen considerably as the horizon extends, which is entirely expected from a statistical standpoint. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 6.6 units, reflecting relatively tight constraints from overnight liquidity conditions and the dampening effect of short-term mean reversion. By one week, the interval nearly doubles to 13 units, as event risk accumulates — scheduled data releases, central bank communications, or geopolitical developments can all compound. At one month, the interval stretches to 27 units, acknowledging that a full month provides ample time for regime shifts, sentiment changes, or surprise shocks to fundamentally alter the trajectory.

Specific risks that could push outcomes beyond the stated intervals include sudden policy pivots from major central banks, particularly unexpected rate decisions or forward guidance changes that markets have not priced in. On the downside, a sharp deterioration in risk sentiment — triggered by a financial stability event, a geopolitical escalation, or a worse-than-expected growth print — could drive prices well below the lower bound of even the one-month interval. Conversely, a coordinated positive surprise, such as a ceasefire announcement, a stronger-than-expected economic data cluster, or a significant liquidity injection, could push prices above the upper bounds.

It is also worth acknowledging that my confidence intervals, while calibrated to 90%, are not immune to model error. They implicitly assume a relatively stable volatility regime and no fat-tail discontinuities. In practice, markets occasionally experience gap moves — flash crashes, circuit breaker events, or weekend gaps following unexpected news — that are structurally outside what any smoothly parameterized model would assign meaningful probability to. These tail events, though rare, represent the most serious risk of the stated intervals proving inadequate.
